title: Heredity

toc.title: 4.2 Cell division (mitosis and meiosis), chromosomes, DNA, RNA and genes

html:
Why do you have your mother's eyes or your father's curly hair? Why do two children of the same parents look alike, but not exactly the same?

The passing of characters from parents to their children is called heredity, and the study of heredity and variation is called genetics. Genetics began in a monastery garden with an Austrian monk who grew peas.

This unit explains his experiments and laws, how chromosomes and genes carry the characters, how the sex of a child is decided, and some diseases that run in families.

What the SEE paper expects from this unit

Most marks come from crosses: a monohybrid cross with the 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio and a dihybrid cross with the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio, drawn with a Punnett square (4 marks).

Also expect definitions (heredity, gene, allele, dominant, recessive, genotype, phenotype), the XX-XY mechanism of sex determination, and the cause of Down's syndrome, haemophilia and colour blindness.

4.1 Mendel's experiments and laws

Heredity and variation

Heredity

Heredity is the transmission of characters (traits) from parents to offspring through genes.

Variation is the difference between individuals of the same species, even between brothers and sisters. Variation arises because the offspring receive a mixture of genes from two parents and because of changes in genes called mutations.

Variation helps a species to survive when the environment changes.

Gregor Johann Mendel

Gregor Johann Mendel (1822–1884) was an Austrian monk. Between 1856 and 1863 he did experiments on the garden pea (Pisum sativum) in the garden of his monastery in Brno (now in the Czech Republic) and published them in 1866.

His work was not noticed until 1900, when three scientists (de Vries, Correns, Tschermak) found his results independently. Mendel is called the father of genetics.

Why did Mendel choose the pea plant?

  • It has clear, contrasting characters (tall or dwarf, round or wrinkled seed).
  • It is self-pollinating, so pure lines (true-breeding plants) are easy to get, but it can also be cross-pollinated by hand.
  • Its life cycle is short and it produces many seeds.
  • It is easy to grow and the flowers are large enough to handle.

Mendel studied seven pairs of contrasting characters:

Character Dominant form Recessive form
Height of stem Tall Dwarf
Seed shape Round Wrinkled
Seed colour Yellow Green
Pod shape Inflated (full) Constricted
Pod colour Green Yellow
Flower colour Violet (purple) White
Flower position Axial (along the stem) Terminal (at the tip)

Terms used in genetics

Term Meaning
Character / trait A feature that can be inherited, e.g. height
Gene A segment of DNA on a chromosome that controls a character
Allele One of the alternative forms of a gene (T for tall and t for dwarf)
Dominant An allele that shows its effect even when only one copy is present (capital letter)
Recessive An allele that shows its effect only when two copies are present (small letter)
Homozygous (pure) Two identical alleles: TT or tt
Heterozygous (hybrid) Two different alleles: Tt
Genotype The genetic make-up of an organism (TT, Tt, tt)
Phenotype The visible character (tall, dwarf)
Hybrid Offspring of parents that differ in one or more characters
P generation Parental generation
F₁ and F₂ First and second filial generation (children and grandchildren)

Monohybrid cross

A monohybrid cross studies the inheritance of one pair of contrasting characters.

Mendel crossed a pure tall plant (TT) with a pure dwarf plant (tt).

  • The F₁ generation: all plants were tall. The dwarf character seemed to have disappeared.
  • He then let the F₁ plants self-pollinate. The F₂ generation had both tall and dwarf plants in the ratio 3 : 1: about 787 tall and 277 dwarf in his counts.

So the dwarf character was not lost; it was hidden in F₁.

Explanation: A pure tall plant (TT) makes only T gametes; a pure dwarf (tt) makes only t gametes. Every F₁ plant is Tt, and shows tall because T is dominant. Tt plants make two kinds of gametes, T and t, in equal numbers. They combine at random:

Gametes T t
T TT (tall) Tt (tall)
t Tt (tall) tt (dwarf)
  • Phenotypic ratio F₂: 3 tall : 1 dwarf.
  • Genotypic ratio F₂: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.

Worked example 4.1 (monohybrid cross with round and wrinkled seeds)

Problem. A pea plant heterozygous for round seeds (Rr) is self-pollinated, and 400 seeds are produced. Round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r). How many seeds are expected to be round and how many wrinkled?

Solution. Gametes of Rr: R and r. Punnett square: RR, Rr, Rr, rr.

Phenotypic ratio = 3 round : 1 wrinkled.

Round seeds = 3/4 × 400 = 300. Wrinkled seeds = 1/4 × 400 = 100.

Genotypes: 100 RR, 200 Rr, 100 rr.

Test cross

A tall plant may be TT or Tt. To find its genotype, it is crossed with a recessive (dwarf, tt) plant. This is the test cross.

  • If all offspring are tall, the plant tested was TT (homozygous).
  • If half tall and half dwarf (1 : 1), the plant was Tt (heterozygous).

Dihybrid cross

A dihybrid cross studies the inheritance of two pairs of contrasting characters at the same time.

Mendel crossed a pure plant with round yellow seeds (RRYY) with a pure plant with wrinkled green seeds (rryy).

  • F₁: all plants had round yellow seeds (RrYy).
  • F₂ (by self-pollination of F₁): four kinds of seeds in the ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

Each F₁ plant (RrYy) makes four kinds of gametes in equal numbers: RY, Ry, rY, ry. The 16 combinations are shown in the Punnett square:

RY Ry rY ry
RY RRYY RRYy RrYY RrYy
Ry RRYy RRyy RrYy Rryy
rY RrYY RrYy rrYY rrYy
ry RrYy Rryy rrYy rryy

Counting the phenotypes:

Phenotype Number of boxes
Round yellow 9
Round green 3
Wrinkled yellow 3
Wrinkled green 1

Two new combinations (round green and wrinkled yellow) appeared that were not in either parent. This shows that the two characters are inherited independently.

Worked example 4.2 (dihybrid cross numbers)

Problem. In a dihybrid cross RrYy × RrYy, 1,600 seeds are produced. How many are expected to be(a) round yellow,(b) wrinkled green,(c) round green?

Solution. Ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, total 16 parts. One part = 1,600 / 16 = 100 seeds.

(a) Round yellow = 9 × 100 = 900.

(b) Wrinkled green = 1 × 100 = 100.

(c) Round green = 3 × 100 = 300.

Check: 900 + 300 + 300 + 100 = 1,600.

Mendel's laws of inheritance

  1. Law of dominance. When two pure parents with contrasting characters are crossed, only one character, the dominant one, appears in F₁. The other, the recessive, is hidden.
  2. Law of segregation (law of purity of gametes). The two alleles of a gene separate (segregate) from each other during the formation of gametes, so each gamete carries only one allele of each gene.
  3. Law of independent assortment. When two or more pairs of characters are inherited together, the alleles of each pair separate independently of those of the other pair. This gives new combinations such as round green and wrinkled yellow.
Common mistake

The 3 : 1 ratio is the phenotypic ratio; the genotypic ratio is 1 : 2 : 1. Many students write the wrong one. Also, dominant does not mean "more common" or "stronger"; it only means that the character shows when the allele is present with a recessive one.

Incomplete dominance

Sometimes neither allele is fully dominant. In the four o'clock plant (Mirabilis jalapa), a cross between red (RR) and white (rr) flowers gives pink (Rr) flowers in F₁. In F₂ the ratio is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.

This is incomplete dominance, and here the phenotypic and genotypic ratios are the same.

4.2 Cell division (mitosis and meiosis), chromosomes, DNA, RNA and genes

Cell division: Amitosis, Mitosis and Meiosis (CDC Grade 10 focus)

Living organisms grow, repair damaged tissues and reproduce through cell division — the process by which a parent (mother) cell divides into new daughter cells.

Each division consists of karyokinesis (division of the nucleus) followed by cytokinesis (division of the cytoplasm).

Aside from primitive amitosis (direct division in bacteria, amoeba and yeast), eukaryotic cells divide by two main methods:

Basis Mitosis (Equational / Somatic Cell Division) Meiosis (Reductional / Reproductive Cell Division)
Where it occurs Occurs in somatic (body) cells and vegetative parts (stem tip, root tip, skin, bone marrow) Occurs in diploid germ (reproductive mother) cells in testes and ovaries (and anthers/ovules of flowers)
Number of divisions Completed in one division (Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase) Completed in two successive divisions: Meiosis I (reductional) and Meiosis II (equational)
Number of daughter cells One mother cell produces two daughter cells One mother cell produces four daughter cells (gametes/spores)
Chromosome number Remains unchanged / diploid (2n \rightarrow 2n; in humans 46 \rightarrow 46); hence called equational division Reduced to half / haploid (2n \rightarrow n; in humans 46 \rightarrow 23); hence called reductional division
Crossing over & variation No crossing over; daughter cells are genetically identical to the mother cell and to each other Crossing over occurs at chiasmata in Prophase I, exchanging genetic segments and producing genetic variation
Main significance Physical growth, healing of wounds, tissue regeneration, genetic stability and asexual reproduction Forms haploid gametes (sperm and ovum), keeps species chromosome number constant across generations, and brings variation/evolution

Difference between DNA and RNA

Basis DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid) RNA (Ribonucleic Acid)
Structure Double-stranded antiparallel helix (Watson and Crick model) Single-stranded nucleotide chain
Pentose sugar Deoxyribose sugar (\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_4) Ribose sugar (\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_5)
Nitrogenous bases Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C) and Thymine (T) (\text{A}=\text{T}, \text{G}\equiv\text{C}) Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C) and Uracil (U) (in place of Thymine)
Location Primarily inside the nucleus (chromosomes), plus mitochondria and chloroplasts Synthesised in the nucleus (by DNA transcription) and functions in the cytoplasm / ribosomes
Main function Stores and transmits hereditary information from parents to offspring through genes Synthesises proteins (translation via \text{mRNA}, \text{tRNA}, \text{rRNA}) and expresses genetic traits

Where are genes found?

Every cell of a living thing has a nucleus. In the nucleus there are thread-like structures called chromosomes. They are visible as thick rods only when the cell is dividing.

A chromosome is made of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) wound round proteins. A gene is a small section of DNA that has the instruction for making one protein, and so controls one character.

Hierarchy: cell → nucleus → chromosome → DNA → gene.

Chromosome number

Each species has a fixed number of chromosomes. They occur in pairs (one from each parent), called homologous chromosomes.

Organism Number of chromosomes in body cell (2n)
Human 46 (23 pairs)
Pea 14
Maize 20
Rice 24
Housefly 12
Dog 78
Chimpanzee 48

The number of chromosomes does not show the complexity of an organism.

Body cells have two sets of chromosomes (diploid, 2n). Gametes (sperm and egg) have one set (haploid, n). In humans, 2n = 46 and n = 23. When a sperm (n = 23) fuses with an egg (n = 23), the zygote has 2n = 46 again.

In human beings, the 46 chromosomes are 22 pairs of autosomes (control body characters) and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX in female, XY in male).

Chromosomal basis of Mendel's laws

Mendel's "factors" are the genes on chromosomes. The segregation of alleles is explained by the separation of the homologous chromosomes in meiosis, the cell division that makes gametes.

The independent assortment of two characters is explained by the random way different pairs of chromosomes line up and separate. Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri (1902) put forward this chromosome theory of inheritance.

Cell divisions: mitosis and meiosis

Mitosis Meiosis
In body (somatic) cells In reproductive organs, to make gametes
One division Two divisions
2 daughter cells 4 daughter cells
Chromosome number stays the same (2n → 2n) Number is halved (2n → n)
Daughter cells identical to the parent Daughter cells differ (variation)
For growth and repair For sexual reproduction

DNA

DNA was described as a double helix by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953, using the X-ray pictures of Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins. It looks like a twisted ladder.

  • The sides of the ladder are made of alternate sugar (deoxyribose) and phosphate.
  • The rungs are pairs of nitrogen bases: adenine (A) pairs with thymine (T), and cytosine (C) pairs with guanine (G).
  • The order of bases along DNA is the genetic code.

DNA can make an exact copy of itself (replication), so the same instructions pass to new cells. RNA carries the message from DNA to make proteins.

4.3 Sex determination

The sex of a child is decided at the moment of fertilisation by the sex chromosomes.

  • A female has two X chromosomes (XX). All her egg cells carry one X: she makes only one kind of gamete.
  • A male has one X and one Y chromosome (XY). Half of the sperm carry X and half carry Y: he makes two kinds of gametes.

At fertilisation:

  • an X-sperm + X-egg gives XX = a girl;
  • a Y-sperm + X-egg gives XY = a boy.
Egg (from mother) X-sperm Y-sperm
X XX (girl) XY (boy)
X XX (girl) XY (boy)

The chance of a boy or a girl is 50 : 50 (1 : 1) each time, whatever the sex of the earlier children.

Worked example 4.3 (sex of children)

Problem. A couple already have three daughters. What is the probability that the fourth child will be a son? Who decides the sex of a child, the father or the mother?

Solution. Each fertilisation is independent. The sperm that reaches the egg is X or Y with equal chance, so the probability of a son (XY) is 1/2 = 50%, whatever the sex of the earlier children.

All eggs carry X, but sperm carry X or Y, so the father's sperm decides the sex of the child. A mother cannot be blamed for having only daughters.

Sex determination in other animals

In birds, butterflies and some reptiles the male has two similar chromosomes (ZZ) and the female has two different ones (ZW), so the female decides the sex.

In bees, fertilised eggs give females and unfertilised eggs give males (see Unit 3). In some reptiles (turtles, crocodiles) the incubation temperature of the egg decides the sex.

Sex-linked inheritance

Genes on the X chromosome are said to be sex-linked. The Y chromosome is much smaller and carries few of these genes. A man has only one X, so a recessive gene on it shows (there is no second X to hide it).

A woman needs two copies of the recessive allele to show the trait. So these traits are more common in men. A woman with one copy is a carrier: she is normal but can pass the allele to her children.

4.4 Genetic disorders

A genetic disorder is a disease or condition caused by a change in a gene or chromosome and passed on in families. Some are caused by faulty genes; others by a wrong number of chromosomes.

Gene disorders

Colour blindness. The person cannot tell red from green. The gene is recessive and lies on the X chromosome. It is more common in boys (about 8% of men and 0.5% of women).

Haemophilia ("bleeder's disease"). The blood does not clot well, so a small cut can bleed for a long time. It is caused by a recessive gene on the X chromosome. Queen Victoria was a carrier and passed it to many royal families in Europe.

In writing the genotypes, X with the letter C stands for the normal allele and X with the letter c for the colour-blind allele:

Genotype Phenotype
X^{C} Y Normal man
X^{c} Y Colour-blind man
X^{C} X^{C} Normal woman
X^{C} X^{c} Normal woman (carrier)
X^{c} X^{c} Colour-blind woman

Albinism. The person lacks the pigment melanin, and so has very light skin, hair and eyes. It is caused by a recessive gene on an autosome (aa); both parents may be normal carriers (Aa).

Sickle cell anaemia. A recessive autosomal disorder in which haemoglobin is abnormal and red blood cells take a sickle shape, blocking small blood vessels. Common in some parts of Africa and India.

Thalassaemia. An inherited disorder of haemoglobin that causes severe anaemia; it occurs in South Asia, including Nepal, and the main way to prevent it is screening before marriage and genetic counselling.

Worked example 4.4 (carrier mother)

Problem. A normal woman who is a carrier for colour blindness (X^{C} X^{c}) marries a normal man (X^{C} Y). What are the chances of colour-blind children?

Solution. Gametes of the mother: X^{C} and X^{c}. Gametes of the father: X^{C} and Y.

X^{C} Y
X^{C} X^{C} X^{C} (normal girl) X^{C} Y (normal boy)
X^{c} X^{C} X^{c} (carrier girl) X^{c} Y (colour-blind boy)
  • All daughters are phenotypically normal; half of them are carriers.
  • Half of the sons (1 in 4 of all children) are colour-blind.
  • Overall: 1/4 normal girl, 1/4 carrier girl, 1/4 normal boy, 1/4 colour-blind boy.

Chromosomal disorders

These are due to a change in the number of chromosomes, usually from a mistake in meiosis (non-disjunction), when a pair of chromosomes fails to separate.

Disorder Chromosomes Features
Down's syndrome 47: an extra chromosome 21 (trisomy 21) Short height, flat face, slanting eyes, mental retardation; the risk increases with the age of the mother

Genetic Technology: Selective Breeding, AI, IVF and DNA Testing (CDC Grade 10 focus)

  1. Selective Breeding (Artificial Selection): Choosing parent plants or animals with desirable hereditary traits and breeding them to produce improved offspring: - Inbreeding: Mating closely related individuals of the same breed for several generations to preserve pure traits (though prolonged inbreeding reduces vigour and fertility, called inbreeding depression). - Crossbreeding (Hybridisation): Mating individuals of two different breeds, varieties or species to combine their best qualities (hybrid vigour / heterosis).
    • Textbook examples of hybrids: Mule (Khachchar) — sterile hybrid produced by crossing a male donkey (Equus asinus, 2n=62) and a female horse (Equus caballus, 2n=64) (has 63 chromosomes, combining the horse's size and strength with the donkey's endurance and sure-footedness on mountain trails); Hinny (male horse \times female donkey); Liger / Tigon (lion \times tiger); Pomato (somatic hybrid of potato and tomato); Triticale (wheat \times rye).
  2. Artificial Insemination (AI): Collecting semen from a healthy, high-yielding male bull, preserving it in liquid nitrogen (-196\ ^\circ\text{C}), and introducing it artificially into the reproductive tract of a female at the fertile period to improve livestock breeds rapidly and cheaply.
  3. In Vitro Fertilisation (IVF / "Test-tube Baby"): Fertilising an ovum (egg) with sperm outside the mother's body in a laboratory dish under controlled conditions and transferring the resulting early embryo (zygote/blastocyst) into the mother's uterus to help infertile couples (for example with blocked Fallopian tubes) have a biological child.
  4. Genetic Engineering and DNA Testing (DNA Fingerprinting): - Genetic engineering (recombinant DNA technology): Isolating a desired gene from one organism and inserting it into another organism to produce genetically modified organisms (GMOs / transgenic crops) or medicines such as human insulin manufactured by transgenic bacteria. - DNA testing (DNA profiling / fingerprinting): Because every person (except identical twins) has a unique nucleotide sequence in their DNA and inherits 50\% of their DNA from the mother and 50\% from the biological father, DNA testing is used to settle disputed paternity/maternity, identify criminals from blood, hair or saliva at crime scenes, and identify victims of disasters or air crashes. | Turner's syndrome | 45: one X only (XO), female | Short, no ovaries, infertile | | Klinefelter's syndrome | 47: XXY, male | Tall, small testes, infertile, some breast growth |

Prevention and management

  • Genetic counselling for families with a history of disorders.
  • Avoid marriage between close relatives, since both partners may carry the same harmful recessive gene.
  • Medical tests before and during pregnancy (blood test, ultrasound, amniocentesis) to find disorders early.
  • Healthy living; avoiding smoking, alcohol and radiation during pregnancy reduces some risks.
  • Many genetic disorders cannot be cured, but some can be managed (e.g. giving blood factor to haemophilia patients).

Importance of genetics

  • Agriculture: improved crop varieties (high-yielding rice, maize) and cattle breeds by selecting parents.
  • Medicine: diagnosis, gene therapy and making insulin by genetic engineering.
  • Forensics: DNA fingerprinting to identify criminals and the parents of a child.
  • Conservation: studying the genetic variety of endangered species such as the tiger and rhino.

Chapter summary

  • Heredity is the passing of characters from parents to offspring through genes. Mendel, the father of genetics, worked with pea plants and discovered the laws of inheritance.
  • Monohybrid cross Tt × Tt gives phenotypic ratio 3 : 1 and genotypic ratio 1 : 2 : 1; a test cross with the recessive parent shows whether a dominant plant is pure.
  • Dihybrid cross RrYy × RrYy gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
  • Laws: dominance, segregation (purity of gametes), independent assortment.
  • Cell → nucleus → chromosome → DNA → gene. Humans have 46 chromosomes (22 pairs autosomes + XX or XY). DNA is a double helix with A–T and C–G pairing.
  • Sex is decided by the father's sperm: X-sperm gives a girl, Y-sperm gives a boy; chance 50 : 50.
  • Sex-linked recessive disorders (colour blindness, haemophilia) are commoner in males.
  • Chromosomal disorders: Down's (47, trisomy 21), Turner's (XO, 45), Klinefelter's (XXY, 47). Genetic counselling helps prevention.

Practice questions

Group A — Objective questions (1 mark each)

  1. Who is called the father of genetics? [1]aDarwinbMendelcWatsondLamarck
  2. The genotypic ratio in the F₂ generation of a monohybrid cross is [1]a3 : 1b9 : 3 : 3 : 1c1 : 2 : 1d1 : 1
  3. The sex of a human baby is decided by [1]athe eggbthe spermcthe mother's agedthe food
  4. Down's syndrome is caused by [1]aa missing X chromosomeban extra chromosome 21can extra Y chromosomeda gene on the X chromosome
  5. A plant with the genotype Tt is called [1]ahomozygousbheterozygouscrecessivedpure
  6. The base that pairs with adenine in DNA is [1]acytosinebguaninecthymineduracil
Answers to Group A

1. (b) — Mendel.

2. (c) — 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.

3. (b) — the sperm carries X or Y.

4. (b) — trisomy 21, giving 47 chromosomes.

5. (b) — two different alleles.

6. (c) — A pairs with T (uracil is in RNA).

Group B — Short answer (2 marks each)

  1. Define gene and allele. [2]
  2. Differentiate between genotype and phenotype. [2]
  3. State Mendel's law of segregation. [2]
  4. Why is colour blindness more common in males than in females? [2]
  5. What is a test cross? What is its use? [2]
Answers to Group B

1. A gene is a section of DNA on a chromosome that controls a character. An allele is one of the alternative forms of a gene.

2. Genotype is the genetic make-up (e.g. Tt); phenotype is the visible character (e.g. tall).

3. The two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete gets only one allele.

4. The gene is recessive and on the X chromosome. A male has one X, so one copy of the allele shows; a female needs two copies.

5. A test cross is the cross of an individual with the dominant character with a homozygous recessive individual. It is used to find out whether the individual is homozygous or heterozygous.

Group C — Long answer (4 marks each)

  1. Explain Mendel's monohybrid cross between pure tall and pure dwarf pea plants up to the F₂ generation with a Punnett square. [4]
  2. In a dihybrid cross of RrYy × RrYy, find the phenotypic ratio. If there are 800 offspring, how many are wrinkled green? [4]
  3. A colour-blind man marries a normal woman who is not a carrier. Find the genotypes and phenotypes of their children. [4]
  4. Explain how the sex of a child is determined in human beings, with a diagram. [4]
Answers to Group C

1. P: TT × tt. Gametes T and t. F₁: all Tt (tall). F₁ self: gametes T, t from each parent; Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt. F₂: 3 tall : 1 dwarf, genotypic ratio 1 : 2 : 1.

2. 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green. Wrinkled green = 1/16 × 800 = 50.

3. Man X^{c} Y, woman X^{C} X^{C}. Gametes: X^{c}, Y and X^{C}. Children: X^{C} X^{c} (carrier girls, normal sight) and X^{C} Y (normal boys). All children have normal sight; the daughters are carriers.

4. Female XX makes eggs with X only. Male XY makes sperms of X and Y in equal numbers. X-sperm + egg = XX girl; Y-sperm + egg = XY boy. The chance is 50 : 50. The father's sperm decides.

Group D — Model answers for long questions (10 marks each, for deeper revision)

  1. State and explain Mendel's law of segregation using a monohybrid cross of tall and dwarf pea plants up to the F2 generation. [10]
  2. Explain how the sex of a child is determined in human beings. Describe Down syndrome, Turner syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome. [10]

Model answer D1: Mendel's monohybrid cross (10 marks)

Introduction. Gregor Johann Mendel (1822-1884), an Austrian monk, is called the father of genetics. He crossed garden pea plants (Pisum sativum) in the monastery garden and counted the offspring.

The pea was a good choice because it grows quickly, has clear contrasting characters (tall and dwarf, round and wrinkled), and can be self-pollinated or cross-pollinated by hand.

A cross that studies one pair of contrasting characters is a monohybrid cross.

The cross. Let T be the gene for tallness (dominant) and t the gene for dwarfness (recessive).

  1. Parent generation (P). A pure tall plant (TT) is crossed with a pure dwarf plant (tt). The tall plant gives only T gametes, the dwarf gives only t gametes.
  2. First filial generation (F1). All plants are tall, with genotype Tt. The dwarf character has not been lost; it is only hidden.
  3. Self-pollination of F1. Tt × Tt. Each plant gives two kinds of gametes, T and t, in equal numbers.
  4. Second filial generation (F2). The gametes combine by chance, as shown in the Punnett square.
T t
T TT (tall) Tt (tall)
t Tt (tall) tt (dwarf)

Results.

Item F2 result
Phenotypic ratio (what is seen) 3 tall : 1 dwarf
Genotypic ratio (genes present) 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt
Example from 400 plants About 300 tall and 100 dwarf

Mendel's laws explained.

  • Law of dominance. When two different alleles are present, only the dominant one shows in the F1 generation (all Tt plants are tall).
  • Law of segregation (purity of gametes). The two alleles of a pair separate during the formation of gametes, so each gamete carries only one allele (T or t). The dwarf character reappears in F2 because t was never lost.

Test cross. To find whether a tall plant is TT or Tt, cross it with a dwarf (tt) plant. If all the offspring are tall, the plant is TT; if half are dwarf, it is Tt.

Conclusion. The 3 : 1 ratio proves that characters are carried by separate units (genes) that pass unchanged from parent to child, and this is the basis of heredity.

Model answer D2: sex determination and chromosomal disorders (10 marks)

Introduction. A human body cell has 46 chromosomes, arranged in 23 pairs. Twenty-two pairs are autosomes and one pair is the sex chromosomes: XX in a female and XY in a male.

Sex determination.

  1. A mother has only X chromosomes, so every egg carries one X.
  2. A father's sperm are of two kinds in equal numbers: half carry X and half carry Y.
  3. If an X-sperm fertilises the egg, the child is XX, a girl. If a Y-sperm fertilises it, the child is XY, a boy.
  4. The chance of a boy or a girl is therefore 50 : 50, and it is the father's sperm that decides the sex. A mother cannot be blamed for the sex of a child.
X (egg) X (egg)
X (sperm) XX girl XX girl
Y (sperm) XY boy XY boy

Here the four squares give 2 girls : 2 boys, which is the 1 : 1 ratio.

Chromosomal disorders. These arise when a cell gets too many or too few chromosomes, usually because chromosomes fail to separate during the formation of the egg or sperm.

Disorder Chromosomes Cause Features
Down syndrome 47, an extra chromosome 21 (trisomy 21) Non-separation of chromosome 21 Slow mental growth, short height, slanting eyes, flat face, heart defects
Turner syndrome 45, XO female One X chromosome is missing Short height, no ovary development, so no periods and no children
Klinefelter syndrome 47, XXY male An extra X chromosome Tall body, small testes, little sperm, often sterile

Karyotype. A karyotype is a picture of all the chromosomes of a person, arranged in pairs by size. Doctors use it to find these disorders.

Prevention and care. The chance of Down syndrome rises with the mother's age, so regular antenatal check-ups at a health post or hospital are advised. Children with these syndromes can lead meaningful lives with love, education and medical care.

Conclusion. The sex of the child depends on the sperm, and wrong numbers of chromosomes cause syndromes. A karyotype helps in diagnosis.
